The New York Mets are in offseason mode and are lacking a true ace to anchor their starting rotation. Nonetheless, one potential guy could fill that need: Los Angeles Dodgers starter Tarik Skubal.
While New York can spend the money under owner Steve Cohen, the question is whether he and Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns want to commit to the long-term contract and money Skubal will demand.
Although the Mets need an ace, Underscore Media's Sal Licata believes that New York should stay away from Skubal, given that the team will still have significant holes on the roster.
"In this particular spot, do you think Tarik Skubal alone is the difference-maker for the Mets? I don't," Licata said in an Oct. 1 Underscore Media video on X. "I think they need more than one guy atop their rotation, and if you're telling me that there are going to be at least some kind of limitations, and forget the collective bargaining agreement, all that stuff, if there is going to be some kind of limitations.
"There always are; even Steve Cohen has his limit. It's stupid to have the luxury tax threshold and not be able to go out and balance the team out if you need to. You don't want to just go all in on three freaking players. It just doesn't work."
Mets Urged to Follow Yankees Path
Moreover, Licata believes the Mets should take the approach the New York Yankees did when they didn't re-sign Juan Soto and opted to spread that money around rather than pay one guy.
"If that's going to be a thing, then why wouldn't you rather spread that out a little bit?" Licata added. "In theory, do what the Yankees did after they lost out on Soto and spread it out a little bit and allow you to add multiple pieces."
Tarik Skubal Could Pitch in Major Market Like New York
Meanwhile, SNY's Keith Raad says that if the Mets do make a serious run at Skubal in free agency, they wouldn't have to worry about the veteran ace having that shock of pitching in a big market. Skubal spent most of his career with the Detroit Tigers, but his midseason trade to the Dodgers shows he can perform for a team in a big market and with expectations.
"Skubal has been there and done that a little bit, even though he's pitched in Detroit and the fact that he's pitching well for the Dodgers as the guy in the trade shows me that he would be fine," Raad said in an Oct. 1 appearance on SNY.
"The only cautionary tale I would have is, again, Mets in-house; they brought in people, they brought in players that maybe started to go south. They have not been able to get them right. That's the part that the Mets need to figure out in player acquisition. Can we get them back to the back of the baseball card, just a simple average of who they are?"
Since the trade to the Dodgers, Skubal is 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 10 appearances, per StatMuse.

The Yankees made MLB playoff history in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, starting eight true left-handed hitters to face right-handed Boston Red Sox starter Sonny Gray.
Never before had a team started that many lefty batters — not including switch-hitters — in a postseason game, per the Elias Sports Bureau.
“I saw our lineup and I assumed that was probably the case,” one of those lefties, Cody Bellinger, told the Daily News with a grin. “I didn’t know. We’ve got a lot of talent in this locker room.”
It was in stark contrast to Tuesday night’s Game 1, when the Yankees started only four left-handed batters against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle in an eventual 9-0 win in the Bronx.
On Wednesday night, lefty-swinging first baseman Luis García Jr., second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., center fielder Trent Grisham and third baseman Ryan McMahon all returned to the starting lineup as the Yankees sought platoon advantages.
Lefty-hitting Spencer Jones, who started Game 1 in center field, moved to right field for Game 2.
Meanwhile, righty-swinging Paul Goldschmidt, Heliot Ramos, Amed Rosario and Anthony Volpe all began Wednesday’s game on the bench after starting Game 1.
Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. was the only right-handed batter in Wednesday’s lineup.
Gray is actually a bit tougher against lefty batters than righties, but because the Red Sox carry five left-handed relievers, Boone said he liked having a bench full of right-handed batters that he could deploy in the later innings.
The best-of-three Wild Card Series allows for this kind of maneuvering because, given its short nature, teams are able to carry more hitters and be more aggressive with their bench moves.
The Yankees carried 16 position players in the Wild Card Series, compared to just 10 pitchers.
That likely won’t be the case in future rounds, when they would need to use a fourth starting pitcher and cover more innings with their bullpen.
But Games 1 and 2 against the Red Sox showed how the Yankees plan to approach the postseason, with matchups dictating their lineup decisions perhaps more than they have in the past.
“With this group, I feel like it’s going to take everyone,” manager Aaron Boone said Wednesday. “So that’s my plan — day in and day out, it’s going to be a little different, potentially. And that phrase ‘all hands on deck’ certainly applies to us with our team right now.”
The Yankees need to prioritize lineup creativity even more because the matchup-proof Aaron Judge is sidelined indefinitely with a calf strain.
Giancarlo Stanton — who also typically starts against righties and lefties — is currently relegated to pinch-hitting duty after missing more than five months due to three separate calf strains.
And Wednesday marked the first game started by Grisham since Sept. 4, when he suffered a hamstring strain. After being activated for the Wild Card round, Grisham entered Game 1 in the seventh inning as a defensive replacement and went 0-for-1 at the plate.
“I know he’s ready to go,” Boone said. “I liked his at-bat [in Game 1] when he came in, hit a ball well to center. I don’t know what I’m going to get from any of the guys tonight. But I’ve got a lot of confidence in who he is and what he can bring to the table.”
The Yankees became even more platoon-oriented after they acquired García and Ramos, both of whom perform to traditional splits, before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
All of those factors led to Wednesday’s historic, lefty-loaded lineup.
“It’s super beneficial for us, because all the guys in the lineup are super tight — righties and lefties — and there will be a lot of different conversations between different guys in what they saw, how they picked it up,” Jones told The News.
“And then we’ve got a bunch of guys ready to go off the bench.”
SCHMIDT SHUT DOWN
Clarke Schmidt’s season is officially over.
The right-hander has been shut down after landing on the IL with right biceps neuritis shortly after making his long-awaited return from Tommy John surgery.
Boone said last week that it was his understanding Schmidt would be shut down, but he hadn’t confirmed it until Wednesday.
But Boone said Schmidt is doing “fine.” That’s in line with what Boone shared last week, when he said Schmidt was expected to have a normal winter to build up for spring training.
More than a year after undergoing elbow surgery, Schmidt made his season debut on Sept. 16 and recorded two outs in a relief appearance.
A starter by trade, Schmidt had hoped to help out of the Yankees’ bullpen this postseason.
But Schmidt experienced a cramping sensation as he warmed up for a second relief appearance, then returned to the IL last Thursday.
VOLPE NEWS
Volpe has a new agent, confirming to The News that he is now being represented by Scott Boras and the Boras Corporation.
Boras is baseball’s most prolific agent, representing stars such as Juan Soto, Gerrit Cole and Bellinger.
Volpe, 25, is eligible for free agency after the 2028 season.

Apple vs. Microsoft. Coke vs. Pepsi. Marvel vs. DC. Ford vs. General Motors.
All child’s play compared to Yankees vs. Red Sox.
Though seeded as Wild Cards, New York and Boston are heavyweight entries in the 2026 postseason field. And only one can advance out of the best-of-three Wild Card Series that begins -- and takes place entirely -- in the Bronx on Tuesday.
The Yankees have survived most of the season without captain Aaron Judge, while the Red Sox survived a brutal start that had them 14 games under .500 in late June.
But who will survive this short and scintillating series at Yankee Stadium? Let’s break it down, position by position, and we are sure to find the unmistakably correct prediction, right? Right?!
Catcher
Austin Wells just hasn’t produced with the consistency he did in his Rookie of the Year finalist season in 2024 or the power he had in last year’s 20-homer, 20-double campaign. He’s a fantastic framer and blocker, and that could matter more in the postseason than his bat given the pitching staff’s increased importance in a short series. But Rutschman has those same strengths, along with an elite caught stealing track record, to go with higher offensive upside in a season in which he’s posted an above-average OPS+.
Edge: Red Sox
First base
The Red Sox have a major asset, but also a major question mark in Willson Contreras. He was a monumental offseason pickup in a trade with the Cardinals. The veteran produced his best offensive season yet, with an OPS over .900 and career-highs in homers and RBIs.
But when Contreras was plunked in the hand by a pitch late in the regular season, it complicated the equation. As of this writing, it was still not clear if he would suit up for the Wild Card Series. Even if he does, he might need some time to get back in the swing of things, given the impact hand discomfort can have on a power stroke.
So the Yankees’ successful midseason acquisition of Luis García Jr. looms large here. After an offensive breakthrough with the Nationals, he’s remained an above-average producer in pinstripes, finishing off his 30-homer season. And the Yanks have a dangerous platoon option in Paul Goldschmidt, the consummate pro who still does big damage to lefties – no small tool in their chest given the lefty leaning complexion of the Red Sox’s starting staff.
Edge: Yankees
Second base
Between the trade of the disappointing Marcelo Mayer and a late-season injury to Anthony Siegler, the Red Sox are left piecing things together here with Nick Sogard and veteran Isiah Kiner-Falefa, and Sogard’s contact skills can play up in the postseason even if he doesn’t produce much power.
But the Yankees have higher upside here. Though Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s walk year saw statistical regression, he ultimately provided league-average offense with north of 40 steals. He could augment his open-market asking price with a strong showing.
Edge: Yankees
Shortstop
Trevor Story was sidelined for the Sox for about three months with a sports hernia that required surgery. He showed signs of offensive life in September, but this will nevertheless go down as one of his worst seasons at the plate in limited time.
The Yankees look like they have a star in the making in George Lombard Jr. While no one knows how the fresh-faced 21-year-old, who only debuted on Aug. 4, will perform under the bright lights of the postseason, he’s already had some huge hits for the Yanks and his plate discipline, high baseball IQ, fluid actions and plus speed all make him dangerous in a short series.
Edge: Yankees
Third base
The hot corner has been cold to the Yankees this year. Veteran Ryan McMahon’s first full season in the Bronx has been a drastic disappointment and his right-handed-hitting complement Amed Rosario hasn’t been much better. The Yankees were toying with the idea of working former shortstop Anthony Volpe here.
As for Boston, while replacing free-agent departure Alex Bregman was a tall order, a trade for Caleb Durbin, a reigning NL Rookie of the Year finalist with the Brewers, has paid enormous dividends. Durbin looked lost in the headlights for his first couple months in a major market, but his midseason ignition matched that of the club at large. He has great range at third, is among the more difficult batters in MLB to strike out and logged 25 doubles for the second straight season.
Edge: Red Sox
Left field
After getting spurned by Juan Soto in free agency the previous winter, the Yankees did not let Cody Bellinger get away. In his second season with the Yanks, the former NL MVP became an All-Star Game MVP in the midst of providing his usual disciplined, contact-and-power profile at the plate and elite defense in the grass. He’s been on this postseason stage plenty of times before.
There was hope in Boston that Roman Anthony would break out into superstardom this season. But a significant finger ligament injury early in the season got in the way, opening the door for Jarren Duran to see the bulk of time in left while producing an OPS+ more than 20% below league average. Anthony returned in late August, and it should shock no one if this postseason turns into his coming-out party. But for now, we’ve got to go with the more accomplished veteran here.
Edge: Yankees
Center field
The Sox had another late-season health scare with Ceddanne Rafaela, their rangy, speedy power-armed gem in center field. Rafaela was finishing up his finest offensive season to date when he suffered a right quad strain a few weeks back. But a clean MRI in the season’s final week allowed him to return.
Meanwhile, Trent Grisham’s September hamstring strain gave the Yankees their own center-field concern. Grisham’s absence allowed 25-year-old rookie Spencer Jones to showcase his excellent raw power and athleticism. Grisham could be back for this series. But Rafaela’s offensive breakthrough and Gold Glove defense carry the way here.
Edge: Red Sox
Right field
Judge’s calf injury is probably the biggest X-factor in the entire postseason field. The Yankees were cagey about its severity, and manager Aaron Boone said the club was preparing for a Wild Card Series without the captain. Judge was intent on trying to make his way back. But ultimately, Judge was left off the Bombers' Wild Card roster, so they'll be down one of the best hitters on the planet.
For the Red Sox, Wilyer Abreu is ready for his close-up. He was a durable doubles machine who also reached career highs in homers and RBIs, he dramatically improved his production against left-handed pitching, and he has range and a mammoth arm in right. His surge was essential in the Sox returning to the postseason.
Edge: Red Sox
Designated hitter
With Masataka Yoshida out with a hamstring strain, Boston will utilize a DH platoon that includes Roman Anthony against righties and Jahmai Jones against lefties.
In a season that has included so little Judge, the Yankees have gotten a ton out of Ben Rice. Last season’s surprise ascendence for the New England native has proven to be only an appetizer. Rice showed he can mash both lefties and righties alike in clearing the 40-homer threshold, getting selected as a first-time All-Star and earning down-ballot MVP support.
Edge: Yankees
Starting pitching
Cam Schlittler’s likely Cy Young-winning breakthrough in 2026 came on the heels of him carving up the Red Sox club he grew up rooting for in last year’s Wild Card Series. He pairs with Max Fried and Gerrit Cole to give the Yankees a terrifying top end of the rotation in this short series, even if the finish on Cole’s pitches is not yet what it was prior to Tommy John.
While the Yankees deserve the edge here, that’s not to suggest the Sox are slouches in the starting department. That they got to this point essentially without Garrett Crochet took a lot of fortitude, and Payton Tolle’s fantastic rookie campaign was one of the most fun storylines of the season. Sonny Gray remains an absolute command artist in his age-36 season, and Ranger Suarez was a terrific offseason signing who drastically limits the kind of hard contact that can change games in October.
Still, it’s the Yanks here.
Edge: Yankees
Bullpen
These are two top-five relief units in terms of both ERA and expected ERA. Both are excellent at suppressing long balls, which is crucial in October.
The Yankees have a strong ninth-inning anchor in David Bednar, whose elite ability to generate chase with his four-steam/split/curve mix can neutralize even the biggest bats. Paul Blackburn has gone from oft-injured starter to absolute force of nature in the setup role, and Brent Headrick has also undergone a massive transformation as a member of the Yankees ‘pen, for whom he has emerged as a whiff machine. The strength of the starting staff has trickled down to a Yankees bullpen that ranks among the lowest innings workloads of any relief unit in MLB this season.
With Tyron Guerrero’s recent return from injury and the presence of Garrett Whitlock, Greg Weissert and lefty Jovani Morán, the Sox are well-situated in their bridge to the ninth. And in the ninth, they’ve got the ageless Aroldis Chapman, whose age-38 season has seen him produce yet another sub-2.00 ERA, another ERA+ more than 100% better than league average and upper-echelon velo and strikeout rates. He recently returned from a late-season lat issue. Between Chapman’s presence and the possibility that Crochet’s elite arsenal impacts the ‘pen in his potential return from injury, the Red Sox earn the edge.
Edge: Red Sox
Prediction
The Yankees were the better team in record and run differential, and they did it mostly without Judge. They hold the home-field and rotation advantages, have a higher run-scoring baseline and are, therefore, the clear favorites.
All reasons why I’m taking the Red Sox in three. Because baseball.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Days before the start of what could be Major League Baseball's last postseason for a while, Carlos Rodon was prepared for a long lockout if owners keep their salary cap proposal on the bargaining table.
"We won't play. I'm going to be frank with you," the New York Yankees pitcher said. "I'm not worried about it. They should be worried about it. There's a lot of money on us playing baseball. That's why they pay us a lot."
Baseball's five-year labor contract expires Dec. 1 and management is expected to impose a lockout that would stop trades and free-agent signings, then potentially threaten the start of spring training workouts on Feb. 9 and opening day on March 24.
When management last proposed a cap, it sparked a 7 1/2-month strike in 1994 and '95 that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years. MLB says a cap is needed to alleviate economic disparity, highlighting that no low-revenue team has won the title since the 2015 Kansas City Royals.
"The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said.
Owners would also gain more financial certainty with a cap, which likely would spark an increase in franchise values.
Players point out teams with low payrolls, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, had the best regular-season records in their leagues this season.
"Despite MLB claiming they need a salary cap because small-market teams supposedly have no hope, we see Milwaukee with the best record in baseball for the second straight year and Tampa with the best record in the AL," union head Bruce Meyer said. "Milwaukee, of course, is 30th out of 30 in our market-size rankings."
While this would be MLB's 10th work stoppage, the sport hasn't lost any regular-season games since the 1994-95 strike. Baseball players say they will never accept a cap similar to those that have been in the NFL since 1994, the NBA since 1984-85 and the NHL since 2005-06. Nine of the 10 biggest sports contracts by total value in North America belong to MLB players.
"For me the biggest thing is doing right for the generations forward because the generations before me, for the decades before, they've fought for our rights today," Baltimore first baseman Pete Alonso said. "That's a sacrifice that not just myself but other men around the league are willing to fight for and put up with."
MLB's proposal would cap team spending next year at $245.3 million, using figures for luxury tax payrolls that include an estimated $23 million for benefits and the pre-arbitration bonus pool. It also would establish a payroll floor of $171.2 million for 2027 but teams could drop as low as $154.1 million and make up the difference over the following two years. The New York Mets' opening day payroll in 2026 was more than $352 million.
Contracts would be limited by service time: $500 million and 12 years for those yet to make major league debuts down to $265 million and six years for free-agent-eligible players. It would outlaw megadeals like outfielder Juan Soto's record 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets.
While MLB proposed to split revenues 50-50, the union says that would lead to a massive decrease in money to players because of the way revenues and expenses are defined and the player portion is calculated. In addition, an escrow provision to set salaries aside in case the players' defined revenue share is above 50% means money in guaranteed contracts could be forfeited.
MLB as part of a cap system would agree to drop service time for free agent eligibility for some players from six years of service to five and to eliminate qualifying offers, but the union maintains that would shift money among players under a cap rather than increase spending.
Alonso would lose $165,775 next year for each regular-season day missed and Rodon would forfeit $144,385.
Los Angeles Dodgers star Shohei Ohtani would give up $374,331 daily and Soto $227,273.
At the other end of the salary scale, players making MLB's proposed $900,000 minimum would lose $4,813 daily. Among the 1,366 players on rosters as of Monday, 549 (40%) started 2026 with less than one year of service time and 893 (65%) had less than three years. Players aren't eligible for salary arbitration until they've completed three seasons, with some exceptions.
Some players are protected financially because of signing bonuses that will continue to be paid during a work stoppage: Toronto first baseman Vladimir Guerrero Jr. is due $14 million on June 30 as part of his $325 million contract, though he would give up $74,866 daily in salary.
Tony Clark, the former All-Star first baseman who had headed the union since 2013, was forced out in February and replaced by Meyer, his deputy and chief negotiator in 2021-22.
Baltimore pitcher Chris Bassitt, a member of the union's eight-man executive subcommittee, said there had been a transformation this year in communications within the players' association. The subcommittee and the 30 team player representatives form the executive council that makes union decisions.
"Our last CBA from a player's side was not internally handled great. I think the structure was very archaic, so to speak, like an old-school approach," he said. "We have made it our mission to kind of get all 30 clubs -- 30 reps that genuinely care. And then not just 30 reps that genuinely care, but 30 reps that are making sure all their players are very informed."
When players and MLB agreed to a deal on March 10, 2022, that ended the lockout, the executive subcommittee voted 8-0 against accepting it, but the team player representatives favored the agreement by 26-4.
The vast majority of the 1,200 players on 40-man rosters when the lockout starts will not have salary arbitration or free agency rights and will have 2027 salaries under $1 million.
"Their voices matter, what they're feeling, what they're thinking," Bassitt said. "When I came in the league it was -- I'm going to say it plainly -- but it was like: 'Rookie shut up and sit in the corner and the veterans are going to take care of this.' I don't think that's a possible avenue to go down anymore. I think the league's too young, first and foremost. Second, I think the only way to have veteran guys that are informed and understand the process is to start the education process from day one."

The 2026 MLB season is over for the New York Mets, and now they are in offseason mode. One major question mark hanging over the Mets is whether or not infielder Bo Bichette will opt out of his contract.
Bichette’s current contract with the Mets sees him earn $42 million per year over the next two years, per Spotrac. Nonetheless, the question is whether the veteran produced enough this season for another team to pay him more.
In the 2026 season, a batting average of .260 with 166 hits, 18 home runs, 78 RBIs, and 76 runs scored in 160 games, per StatMuse. With an offseason decision looming for Bichette, SNY’s MLB insider Chelsea Janes shared her outlook on how this situation will play out.
“[Juan Soto] and [Francisco] Lindor certainly talked like guys who really wanted Bo Bichette back and have probably communicated that to him,” Janes said during a Sept. 28 appearance on “Baseball Night in New York.”
“I think Bo Bichette stays. I expect him and his agent to kind of let it play out a little bit, make it seem like they get a feel for the market, just kind of make sure that no one’s going to change his thinking.”
Insider Shares Few Other Reasons Bo Bichete Will Stay
Moreover, aside from Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor potentially being in Bichette’s ear telling him to stay, Janes also noted two other reasons why she believes the Mets infielder will remain in New York and not opt out of his contract.
“He settled in here, and he came here for a reason,” Janes added. “I believe what Bo Bichette said early on, that he understands what New York is, and he wants to succeed here. So I think he’s now comfortable. Frankly, his numbers just weren’t that good. It’s not a platform year. So it was $42 million and try again. I think it’s now a bit of a no-brainer.”
Bo Bichette Urged to Remain With Mets for 2027 Season
Recently, John Harper of SNY urged Bichette to remain with the Mets and not opt out of his contract. Harper believes that if the infielder decides to test the market again, no team will give him more than the $42 million per year he’s earning in New York.
Moreover, there’s a potential lockout looming, so it might be in Bichette’s interest to stay with the Mets and possibly test the market next year if he has a better season, given that his three-year contract has opt-outs after each of the first two seasons.
“You’ve got the lockout coming,” Harper said in a Sept. 11 video on SNY’s YouTube channel. “You’re not sure what the salary structure is going to look like, if there’s a cap or not. I think that’s part of it too. [Bichette] has been good since the terrible start, but I was looking at it, and he’s not a superstar. He’s a really good offensive player [and] has got an under .800 OPS in the second half, when he’s done most of his best hitting.
“He doesn’t hit for a lot of power [and] he’s been a clutch guy again since the bad start, hitting almost .300 with runners in scoring position. To me, [$84 million] for the next two years; you can go out in the market after that [but] you’re not getting [$42 million] a year anymore. Now you’re getting a longer contract, but I would stick it out for these two years and then maybe take my chance.”

item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to this season’s final edition of Monday Stat Party, a weekly series showcasing some of the most curious and nostalgia-inducing statistical developments from the past week of Mets baseball. What unites each entry is the sense of intrigue which they aim to spark, and the unbridled love of the game’s anomalies from which they arise. Without further ado, let the stat party begin.
TUESDAY
With his 25th stolen base of the season, A.J. Ewing broke Mookie Wilson’s 1981 record for the most stolen bases by a rookie in franchise history.
Kodai Senga became one of just 11 Japanese-born players to reach eight career saves, joining: Kazuhiro Sasaki (129), Koji Uehara (95), Takashi Saito (84), Akinori Otsuka (39), Shigetoshi Hasegawa (33), Shingo Takatsu (27), Hideki Irabu (16), Hisanori Takahashi (10), Masanori Murakami (9), and Yoshihisa Hirano (8).
Francisco Alvarez and Carson Benge each hit two doubles, marking the first time multiple Mets hit multiple doubles in a game since Ronny Mauricio and Jeff McNeil did it on July 27, 2025, in San Francisco.
WEDNESDAY
Marcus Semien hit his 15th home run of the year, giving the Mets six or more players with 15+ homers for the fifth time in franchise history after 2000 (7), 2017 (8), 2019 (6), and 2025 (6). The only teams with more 15-homer players this season were the Cubs, Reds, and Dodgers (all tied at 7). Of the Mets’ players with 15+ homers last season and this season, only two (Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto) overlap.
Juan Soto reached base four times for the 103rd time in his career, moving past Ted Williams for the third-most such games by a player before turning 28 years old. Soto trails only Mickey Mantle (121) and Jimmie Foxx (112).
Soto became the fifth Met to get intentionally walked three times in a game, after Claudell Washington (August 26, 1980), Vince Coleman (August 10, 1992), Todd Hundley (June 28, 1997), and David Wright (May 19, 2007, and July 18, 2009).
Brett Baty’s 455-foot home run tied the longest blast of his big league career, a homer off Brad Lord on August 20, 2025, in Washington.
Francisco Alvarez’s seventh-inning single registered an exit velocity of 113.7 mph. It was Alvarez’s 15th career batted ball with an exit velocity of 112+ mph, the second-most by a Met player in the Statcast era (since 2015) behind Pete Alonso, who had a whopping 130.
Alvarez, Lindor, and Baty each recorded a batted ball with an exit velocity over 110 mph, marking the first time the Mets recorded three batted balls with an exit velocity of 110+ mph in the same game since September 10, 2025, in Philadelphia.
Nolan McLean completed his rookie year with a total of 179.2 innings pitched, the most by a Mets rookie since Jae Weong Seo (188.1 in 2003), and 194 strikeouts, the third-most by a Mets rookie behind Dwight Gooden (276 in 1984) and Kodai Senga (202 in 2023).
McLean recorded his 250th strikeout in his 39th career game, tying Jacob deGrom for the fifth-fewest games by a Met to reach that milestone behind Dwight Gooden (29 games), Matt Harvey (34 games), Noah Syndergaard (36 games), and Kodai Senga (38 games).
McLean recorded his 26th game with at least five strikeouts this season, the most by a Mets pitcher since deGrom (29) and Syndergaard (27) in 2019.
McLean became the first rookie with 20 quality starts since the Royals’ Yordano Ventura (22 in 2014). McLean’s 20 quality starts this season were tied with Sonny Gray and Cam Schlittler for fifth-most in the majors behind Cristopher Sánchez (22), Yoshinobu Yamamoto (22), Sandy Alcantara (21), and Michael Wacha (21). McLean also recorded his 21st start of six or more innings pitched this season, the second-most by a Met in a season since 2020, trailing only Chris Bassitt (23 in 2022).
THURSDAY
Zac Thornton’s 63 strikeouts through 15 career games ranks fourth among Mets left-handers, behind Steven Matz (87), Bill Pulsipher (74), and David Peterson (69).
Juan Soto became the second Mets player to get intentionally walked four times in a two-game span, after Travis d’Arnaud did it while batting in the No. 8 spot ahead of Jon Niese and Bartolo Colón on June 1-2, 2014, in Philadelphia.
The Mets scored two or fewer runs through nine innings for the 63rd time this season. That ties 2013 for the most such games the Mets have had in a season in the Wild-Card Era (since 1995).
Over the franchise’s first five trips to Arlington, the Mets are still yet to lose a series on the road against the Rangers. They won two of three in 2003, won two of three in 2011, split a two-game set in 2017, won two out of three in 2024, and won two out of three again in 2026.
FRIDAY
Carson Benge became the first Mets rookie with 20+ homers and 20+ stolen bases in a season.
Benge became just the eighth player in MLB history to join the 20/20 club in their debut season, joining: Jackson Chourio (2024), Anthony Volpe (2023), Bobby Witt Jr. (2022), Julio Rodríguez (2022), Marty Cordova (1995), Ellis Burks (1987), and Mitchell Page (1977). (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Benge recorded his 43rd multi-hit game of the season, breaking Pete Alonso’s 2019 record for the most multi-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
With a pinch-hit single in the eighth inning, Brett Baty extended his career-high 18-game on-base streak. It was snapped with an 0-for-4 performance on Saturday.
Bo Bichette hit his fourth home run at Nationals Park this season, tied for the most by a Mets player in any season on the road against the Nats/Expos. His six extra-base hits trail only David Wright (7) in 2012.
Francisco Lindor didn’t notch his 300th home run on Friday night, but he did record three batted balls in a game at 107+ mph for the first time in the Statcast era (since 2015). Unfortunately for him, only one of the three resulted in a base hit.
The Mets allowed five wild pitches in a game and four wild pitches in an inning for the first time in franchise history.
SATURDAY
Jonah Tong set career highs with nine strikeouts and 19 whiffs in a game.
Mets pitchers recorded 14 or more strikeouts in a game for the 12th time this season, the fourth-most such games in a season in franchise history behind 2021 (19), 2019 (17), and 2022 (17).
With a start at shortstop, Brett Baty became the first Mets player to play six different positions in a season since Jeff McNeil in 2023.
Nate Lavender has recorded 19 scoreless appearances in his first 21 career outings, tied with Jaime Cerda, Erik Goeddel, and Daniel Zamora for the second-most by a Met behind Joe Smith (20).
In the Mets’ penultimate game of the season, their No. 8 and No. 9 hitters hit back-to-back homers (A.J. Ewing and Ronny Mauricio). The 2026 Mets had done that once before — in their first game of the season, when Carson Benge and Francisco Alvarez went deep at Citi Field against the Pirates.
The Mets clinched their sixth consecutive victory in the season series with Washington. Their record against the Nationals is 57-33 over that span.
SUNDAY
Francisco Lindor became the fifth player to hit their 300th career home run while having played at least 50% of their games at shortstop, joining Ernie Banks, Cal Ripken Jr., Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Tejada. (source: Sarah Langs on X) He is also the 11th switch-hitter to reach the 300-homer mark. (source: Sarah Langs on X)
Lindor became one of 27 players with 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases, and the third active player to have reached the milestone along with Andrew McCutchen and Mike Trout. He is the fifth member of that club to have played for the Mets; the others were Willie Mays, Darryl Strawberry, Gary Sheffield, and Carlos Beltrán.
Lindor became the seventh player to hit their 300th home run as a Met, joining Dave Kingman, George Foster, Gary Carter, Mike Piazza, Mo Vaughn, and Curtis Granderson.
Lindor’s 300th homer registered a 110.8-mph exit velocity, marking the third-hardest-hit homer as a right-handed batter in his career. His only harder-hit homer from the right side as a Met came on another afternoon in Washington, when he took MacKenzie Gore deep on August 21, 2025.
Ronny Maurcio became the first Met to hit three consecutive homers out of the No. 9 spot, with two on Saturday and one on Sunday. (source: SNY broadcast)
Carson Benge recorded his 14th three-hit game of the season, extending his record for the most three-hit games by a rookie in franchise history.
Juan Soto holds a 1.101 OPS against the Nationals in 39 games played facing his former team. That’s the third-highest OPS for any player with at least 150 plate appearances against the Nationals/Expos, trailing only Jim Edmonds (1.198) and Todd Helton (1.114).
Miscellaneous Mets stat of the week:
Let’s talk about the rookies.
In Carson Benge, Nolan McLean, A.J. Ewing, and Zac Thornton, the Mets have four rookies with at least 1.5 bWAR*. That’s tied for the most rookies with 1.5+ bWAR* in a season in franchise history, matching the mark from 1983 (Darryl Strawberry, Carlos Diaz, Walt Terrell, and Doug Sisk).
In Benge, McLean, and Ewing, the Mets have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*. Prior to this year, they had never had as many as two such rookies in a single season. In fact, the 2026 Mets are just the third team in the modern era (since 1900) to have three rookies with at least 3.0 bWAR*, joining:
2006 Marlins (4: Hanley Ramírez, Dan Uggla, Josh Johnson, and Aníbal Sánchez)
1989 Orioles (3: Randy Milligan, Bob Milacki, Gregg Olson)
*bWAR separated for position players and pitchers, not cumulative
Thank you for following along all year! Here’s to many more stat parties in 2027…

item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto did not need a long answer when asked why the New York Mets can contend in 2027. After a 74-88 season that kept them out of the MLB playoffs, Soto gave a two-word answer: Carson Benge.
That is quite an endorsement for a rookie who just finished his first major league season.
The Mets entered 2026 with much bigger expectations, but injuries and an inconsistent roster eventually caught up with them. They finished last in the NL East and missed the postseason for the second straight year.
Benge, however, gave the club something it desperately needed: a reason to look forward.
The rookie finished with a .282 batting average, 20 home runs, 65 RBI, 168 hits and 22 stolen bases, according to the supplied 2026 statistics. SNY also reported that Benge became the first Mets rookie to reach 20 home runs and 20 stolen bases.
Juan Soto sees Carson Benge as part of the Mets’ future
Soto’s answer carries even more weight because he knows what the Mets need to fix.
The superstar played 111 games and hit .275 with 27 home runs, 68 RBI, a .393 on-base percentage and a .515 slugging percentage. But two calf injuries cost him significant time during the season, including a lengthy absence in July and August.
Soto has also said the Mets need to be active this offseason and add to their young core. He specifically pointed to Benge and other young players as reasons to believe the organization is moving in the right direction.
That puts plenty of attention on Benge heading into 2027. Not bad for a rookie who just finished his first trip around the league. Queens may have had a rough 2026, but at least Benge gave Mets fans something worth circling on the calendar.
The Mets still have work to do. Soto and Francisco Lindor provide veteran star power, but the pitching staff and overall roster need improvement after a 74-88 finish.
For now, though, Soto has made his choice clear when it comes to the biggest reason for optimism.

All choices will be based on the 2026 regular season, without regard for American League or National League affiliation.

Soto, who missed 51 games due to injury, also put up 3.0 bWAR while hitting .275/.393/.515 with 27 home runs and a 154 OPS+.
Other outfield selections include Pete Crow-Armstrong, Mike Trout, James Wood, and Byron Buxton. Other starting pitcher nominees include Sandy Alcantara, Jacob deGrom, Zack Wheeler, and Tarik Skubal.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Mets' season is ending on Sunday.
They have been out of the playoff picture for a long while, and so the final day of the 2026 MLB regular season is all she wrote for the Mets.
There won't be a lot they want to remember about what happened this year, but one player continued to be a leader as best he could: Francisco Lindor.
That included helping the Mets put up some runs on Sunday. If they were going to have the season end, they might as well hit the ball around the yard a bit more.
Lindor didn't just hit it around, either — he left the yard altogether, and it was a historic moment.
Francisco Lindor Makes Rare History
Lindor's home run on Sunday was a milestone for those who appreciate round numbers: He now has 300 home runs.
It makes Lindor the fourth infielder in MLB history with at least 300 home runs and 200 stolen bases.
Lindor has 219 steals to go with his now-300 homers.
He joins a list that also includes Alex Rodriguez, Jeff Bagwell and George Brett.
A-Rod has the most of both stats on this particular list — he hit 696 home runs and stolen 329 bases.
Bagwell ended his MLB career with 449 homers and 202 steals.
Brett just cleared the steals threshold, too, swiping 201 bags while blasting 317 homers.
Lindor joins two Hall of Famers, as well as one of the most talented players of all time in Rodriguez — whose absence from the Hall of Fame has nothing to do with his ability.
Francisco Lindor Future
The big question entering the offseason with Lindor is whether he'll be with the Mets for the long run.
A season ago, the Mets had a brutal collapse to miss the playoffs in the final week of the season.
This year, the Mets never were really even in the picture.
Yes, that also correlates with the signing of Juan Soto to a mega contract, but Lindor has obviously been a part of it, too.
What are the Mets supposed to do? They know that Lindor is still a special player — just as Soto is. But there also feels like there needs to be a vibes change heading into the 2027 season.
There's the added complication this offseason that there could be a lockout that delays the winter action as well as potentially the start of the 2027 season.
So there will be plenty of talking points beyond Lindor. Still, it's worth considering what his future looks like. He can still get the job done, but the Mets are going to want to be a lot better next season, however they can find a way to do that.

item.content:encoded:
Without Aaron Judge for most of the season, the AL MVP race is wide open. The favorite for much of the year has been Houston Astros slugger Yordan Álvarez, but he's far from a sure thing. The New York Yankees have seen Cam Schlittler's candidacy get more recognition in recent weeks, but there's another Yankee who's being grossly overlooked.
Ben Rice was obviously a breakout star for New York last season, but this year he has reached a new gear. Aaron Boone predicted that Rice would clock 39 dingers this season, which was the total the Dartmouth product was sitting on when the Yankees took on the Tampa Bay Rays on September 23, with five games left to play. Neither team had anything left to play for with playoff positions solidified, so it seemed like a good chance that Rice would finish at that number.
But just like that, the 27-year-old bested his manager when he led off the bottom of the first with a solo shot. That wasn't all, though, as Rice came back up to the plate to lead off the bottom of the fourth and smacked his second tater of the game. He now sits at 41 homers and enters the Yankees' record book as a result.
His 40th blast of the year put him in some elite company in franchise history. Rice became just the eighth Yankee to hit 40 or more homers in a season at age 27 or younger. The rest of the list includes four inner-circle Hall of Famers: Babe Ruth (twice), Lou Gehrig (twice), Mickey Mantle (twice), and Joe DiMaggio. In addition to those four, the other three are former single-season home run king Roger Maris, Juan Soto, and, of course, Judge.
Ben Rice's 40th homer underscores how incredibly valuable he's been to the Yankees in Aaron Judge's absence
MLB.com's latest awards poll has Rice as a distant fifth in the voting, behind Álvarez, Junior Caminero, Bobby Witt Jr., and Schlittler, in that order. There are a few things that don't make much sense here.
Álvarez has been great this year, but there's a narrative among some that he's been Judge-like that just isn't true. Air Yordan has posted a 181 wRC+ through September 23, which is still over 20 points lower than Judge's 203 mark last season, which also happened to be the lowest wRC+ he has put up in any of his three MVP campaigns. That's relevant because he is seeking to become the first full-time DH to take home the honor other than Shohei Ohtani.
As for Caminero, he began generating a lot of MVP buzz with his two walk-off homers in mid-September, as if those wins somehow count more than victories at any other point during the season. More importantly, Rice has caught up to him, as both now have 41 homers. Rice has also surpassed him in on-base percentage (.362 versus .360) and slugging percentage (.537 versus .523).
The DH argument also works against Rice, but only to an extent. He's played 55 games at first base and has mostly ceded playing time in the field to accommodate trade deadline acquisition Luis Garcia Jr. It should also be noted that Caminero isn't a great defensive third baseman and is last among qualifiers at the position with -11 outs above average.
More importantly, there's the Judge factor in all of this. The Astros are on the brink of either missing the playoffs for the second year in a row or winning the most pathetic division in MLB history, dipping under .500 late in the campaign. The Rays have had their big boppers like Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda healthy for most of the year.
Losing a player as singular as Judge is a huge blow to a team, but the Yankees are playoff-bound yet again. Throw in a lengthy absence from Cody Bellinger and the fact that they're starting to print milk cartons with Giancarlo Stanton's face on them, and it's been Rice who has kept the offense afloat all year.
If the point of this exercise is to recognize the player who has been the most valuable, then the loss of Judge looms large. We've had our frustrations, but the Yankees really haven't skipped a beat without Judge and his enormous value. Rice is a big reason why, and while it might not be enough to win him the award, he should be a much larger part of the conversation.

item.content:encoded:
Juan Soto’s trade to the New York Mets was one of the biggest money moments in Major League Baseball history. The four-time All-Star agreed to a 15-year, $765 million deal after the 2024 season, topping Shohei Ohtani’s previous record $700 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers in total contract value. When the deal was finalised in December 2024, MLB dubbed the contract the largest in league history.
But that headline figure is only part of the story. Soto’s deal features a $75 million signing bonus and no deferred money, along with an opt-out after the 2029 season. The New York Mets have a provision that can eliminate that opt-out by increasing the annual value of the last 10 seasons, possibly moving the deal from $765 million to $805 million.
Juan Soto’s Mets contract remains MLB’s defining blockbuster after historic $765 million agreement
The original $765 million agreement for Juan Soto with the New York Mets is a 15-year deal from 2025-39 with an average annual value of $51 million.
When finished, it was the biggest and longest deal in MLB history and raised the bar for what free agents could get paid.
The deal came after Soto had finished the 2024 season with the New York Yankees. In his only season in the Bronx, Soto hit .288 with a .419 on-base percentage and .569 slugging percentage, belting 41 homers and scoring 109 runs in 157 games.
He was also third in MVP voting in the American League.
| Contract detail | Juan Soto |
| Team | New York Mets |
| Contract length | 15 years |
| Total value | $765 million |
| Average annual value | $51 million |
| Signing bonus | $75 million |
| Contract period | 2025–2039 |
| Deferred compensation | None |
| Player opt-out | After 2029 season |
| Potential maximum value | $805 million |
The $765 million headline immediately established a new standard for MLB free-agent contracts. Juan Soto surpassed Shohei Ohtani’s $700 million deal with the Los Angeles Dodgers that was signed after the 2023 season. MLB called Soto’s contract the largest free agent deal in league history in total value.
The comparison is further complicated by the timing of payment and the average annual value. Soto’s original deal has an AAV of $51 million, and Ohtani’s $700 million contract has an AAV of $70 million on paper. But Ohtani’s deal has a lot of deferred compensation, so the timing of payments is fundamentally different from Soto’s contract.
Juan Soto and New York Mets built-in contract protections
One of the more unusual aspects of Juan Soto’s deal is the opt-out after the 2029 season. Soto can invoke the clause after five seasons with the New York Mets, and potentially hit the free-agent market at age 31.
But the Mets have a contractual mechanism to prevent the opt-out. The opt-out can be voided if the club increases the average annual value of the final 10 years from $51 million to $55 million. That would push the total contract value to $805 million and the effective AAV over the life of the full deal to roughly $53.67 million.
Another key part of the deal is the $75 million signing bonus. Combined with the salary structure, it adds to the overall value of the deal and makes the contract very different from a simple 15-year salary deal. MLB reported the signing bonus along with the lack of deferred money when describing the deal.
There are financial incentives in Juan Soto’s contract based on performance on top of the guaranteed money. Reportedly includes bonuses tied to National League MVP voting, which adds another layer to the financial structure.
Reported incentives include $500,000 for Soto's first National League MVP award, with bigger bonuses for subsequent MVP wins. There are also bonus payments to high finishers in the voting, including a reported $350,000 for second and $150,000 for a third through fifth place finish.
Juan Soto’s deal compared with Shohei Ohtani’s record
Juan Soto’s New York Mets contract and Shohei Ohtani’s Los Angeles Dodgers deal are two different takes on baseball’s new mega-contracts. The total value of Soto’s deal is bigger, but Ohtani’s contract has a higher stated AAV.
| Financial comparison | Juan Soto | Shohei Ohtani |
| Team | New York Mets | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| Contract length | 15 years | 10 years |
| Total value | $765 million | $700 million |
| Stated AAV | $51 million | $70 million |
| Deferred compensation | None | Significant deferrals |
| Signing year | 2024 | 2023 |
Soto’s 15-year, $765 million contract is higher in total value than Ohtani’s 10-year, $700 million deal, according to MLB’s historical contract records. Soto also set a new record for the longest MLB contract, and Ohtani's deal remains one of the most financially unique because of its extensive deferral structure.
The difference in length of the contract is very important. Soto is signed through 2039, meaning the New York Mets get a long-term commitment for one of the best hitters in baseball. Ohtani’s Dodgers contract is for 10 years, through 2033, but it’s structured to push most of the money into the future.
Juan Soto’s New York Mets contract sets a new benchmark
Soto’s deal also fits into a larger trend of ever-growing MLB contracts. Aaron Judge’s nine-year, $360 million deal with the New York Yankees had set the free-agent standard after the 2022 season, before Ohtani signed his $700 million deal. Soto then added $65 million in total guaranteed value to the ceiling.
Soto’s deal is notable for reasons beyond the record-shattering headline and its contract structure. It’s a 15-year deal with a $75 million signing bonus, no deferred money, an opt-out provision and a possible $805 million escalator, all of which combine to make it a contract unlike the typical long-term MLB contract.
The pact binds the New York Mets deep into the next decade. For Juan Soto, it provides a huge guaranteed money platform with a possible decision point after the 2029 season. That’s why the financial specifics of the deal have been a hot topic throughout MLB, blending long-term security with contractual flexibility.

What became a disastrous season for the New York Mets will mercifully come to an end this coming Sunday afternoon.
While speaking with Mike Puma of the New York Post following the Mets' 3-1 loss at the Texas Rangers on Thursday, star outfielder Juan Soto pointed a finger at himself for the current state of the club.
"It’s definitely not what I imagined in my head," Soto said about the Mets' campaign, per Phillip Martinez of SNY. "There is nothing I can do other than blame myself. I have got to be better. I have got to be at the level to take us forward."
Soto and shortstop Francisco Lindor were supposed to help carry the Mets after team president of baseball operations David Stearns controversially dismantled the core of the club's roster last offseason. Instead, separate calf injuries limited Soto to just 108 games through Thursday afternoon. Over those contests, he slashed .274/.393/.522 with an OPS of .915, 27 home runs and 68 RBI.
That said, Soto is optimistic about the future of a team that features young talents such as Carson Benge, fellow outfielder A.J. Ewing, potential ace Nolan McLean, starting pitcher Christian Scott and others.
"We have a young core, and we have got to maintain that young core and encourage them to the right way, the right path for the future," Soto explained. "I think we are going in the right direction. Look at the young core and what they have been doing their first year in the big leagues. I think it’s real special. It’s always the first and second years are probably the toughest ones of your career, so what they’re doing, I think, is very special."
One can only guess what MLB will look like whenever the expected work stoppage comes to an end, and it's unclear how uncertainty related to the state of the league will impact what clubs do this coming fall. Soto made it clear that he wants Stearns and big-spending Mets owner Steve Cohen to be aggressive in an attempt to engineer a quick turnaround for the franchise.
"We should go and get as much as we can," Soto added. "We need as much help as we can get. It was a real tough year for us, so I think we have got to go out there and grab as much as we can."
The 73-86 Mets will begin a season-closing three-game series at the rival Washington Nationals (75-84) on Friday evening.

Juan Soto has been around the big leagues for long enough to almost forget just how young he is.
Soto is in his ninth big league season, and yet he is somehow still just 27 years old. In comparison, New York Mets rookie starter Nolan McLean is 25 years old, and that's not a wild number, by any means. Soto is an anomaly, and it's why the Mets handed him a mammoth 15-year, $765 million deal ahead of the 2025 season.
With the Mets struggling throughout the season, Soto's greatness likely hasn't been talked about as much as it probably should. But this guy is special. One stat that jumps out is the fact that he's one of just five players in big league history with 250 or more homers and more walks than strikeouts before his 28th birthday, along with Albert Pujols, Mel Ott, Eddie Mathews and Jimmie Foxx, as shared on X by RotoBaller's Eric Cross.
Juan Soto Is Putting Himself Up There With The Greats
That's three Hall of Famers and Pujols, who will be in the second that he's eligible. If Soto can keep this up, he's well on his way as well.
On Thursday, Soto went 0-for-3 with a walk. For his career, Soto has 271 long balls and 972 walks, to just 897 strikeouts in 1,204 games played. He's not going to turn 28 years old until October 25. On the season, the young superstar is slashing .274/.393/.522 with 27 homers and 68 RBIs in 108 games played. The only thing that has slowed him down this season is injuries, and yet he has still had a good overall season. Over the last two seasons, he hit over 40 homers and drove in over 100 runs in at least 157 games. His numbers so far this season are on pace with his last few, if he didn't get hurt.
There are few guys in big league history who have been able to start a career like Soto has. He's a five-time All-Star, six-time Silver Slugger Award winner, one-time batting champ, one-time Home Run Derby champ and a World Series champion. And, again, he's just 27 years old. He should just get better.
He's already etched his name onto plenty of historic lists and the scary thing is the fact that realistically, we may not have seen his best yet. Theoretically, he should be just starting to enter his prime, and yet he's already historic.

Greatest is something every player who wears a New York Mets uniform strives for. Many come and go and are either forgotten about entirely or stick somewhere in the franchise’s lore for having one amazing moment. Fans know Mike Baxter for saving Johan Santana’s no-hitter. They’ll recall the name Mackey Sasser for the inability to throw the ball back to the pitcher safely. Kirk Nieuwenhuis had his random 3-home run game. Luis Castillo lives on in infamy for dropping a routine pop up at Yankee Stadium to end the night.
A mix of greatness and defeat have followed the Mets since they were officially born for the 1962 MLB season. Several Hall of Famers have come through to call the Polo Grounds, Shea Stadium, and Citi Field home. Everything from a mix of the homegrown talent of Tom Seaver to the ill-fated signing of Justin Verlander have a part in Mets history.
While some players live on forever with statues or their numbers retired, so do individual seasons. Random, expected, and in other seasons a longtime coming, these 25 individual seasons by Mets players are the greatest in the franchise’s history. You can’t think of these players without recalling how impressive of a year they had.
The 25 best seasons by Mets players in franchise history
25) Gary Carter, 1985
Gary Carter’s entrance into Mets lore began with a bang. Literally. He homered on Opening Day 1985 and would continue to pummel baseballs throughout the season for his new ball club. Carter finished with a 6.9 bWAR (what does that mean in 1985?) plus 32 home runs and 100 RBI. Exactly matching the .853 OPS he had in his final year with the Montreal Expos the year prior, it was the early telltale sign the Mets made the right decision to make him a part of their core. Partly because the Mets made the playoffs the next year, Carter was able to jump from sixth to third in the MVP vote. Despite this, his 1985 season was the better one.
24) Cleon Jones, 1969
Offense isn’t what won the Mets the 1969 World Series. The hitting was okay, but for the longest time, Cleon Jones’ .340 batting average sat well above anyone else in franchise history. Worth 7 bWAR in part because of an atypical season where he actually rated positively as a defender, Jones had an often-overlooked year where he finished 7th in the NL MVP vote. In an era when pitching dominated, Jones’ season deserves more credit. The year might not compare as well as some Mets years with 30+ home runs or 100+. However, for the timing of when it took place and the well-aged batting average, Jones deserves the accolades.
23) Jesse Orosco, 1983
Spoiler alert! There won’t be another relief pitcher on this list. They’re sometimes hard to judge because of how many fewer innings they throw. Plus, with the ever-evolving usage of arms, they don’t stack up well against each other in different eras. Nevertheless, what Jesse Orosco accomplished in 1983 was outlandish. At 13-7 all out of the bullpen, he tossed 110 innings and had a 1.47 ERA. The effort earned him third place in the NL Cy Young. It was a one-of-a-kind type of season from a Mets reliever. Somewhat unspoken, it was only his second full season as a major league pitcher and already he was at the top of his game while helping to further define the closer role.
22) Jose Reyes, 2006
Several different Jose Reyes seasons deserve to be on this list. How does one differentiate between them? He won a batting title in 2011 but lacked in other areas. In 2006, he hit .300, had a career-best 5.9 bWAR, and stole 64 bases. Most memorable was scoring 122 runs and driving in another 81. Homering 19 times helped make this maybe his most prolific offensive season for New York. The 2006 Mets are remembered for their incredible lineup. Reyes at the very top was one of the biggest factors.
21) Edgardo Alfonzo, 2000
Edgardo Alfonzo is a beloved Mets player. He crosses off a lot of the boxes fans desire. He was homegrown, versatile, and put together some really good years for winning ball clubs. In 2000, he wasn’t the main attraction and yet the season’s totals hold up nicely all of these years later. His lone All-Star season included a career-best 6.4 bWAR with 25 home runs and 94 RBI. Both of those numbers were a little short of what he did the year previous. However, his .967 OPS overpowered any of his past seasons and remains one of the best in Mets history. Alfonzo could be trusted to hit anywhere from first to fifth in the lineup if needed.
20) Lance Johnson, 1996
The 1996 Mets weren’t very good, but they did have three players who hit really well. One of the trio put together a season that landed him on the record books and doesn’t look like it’ll be surpassed. Lance Johnson’s 227 hits and 21 triples both set single-season Mets records while leading the league. In addition to the bat, he stole 50 bases and earned himself a 1.9 dWAR. If we were ranking only seasons by Mets leadoff hitters, this would be right near the top. It’s a shame this couldn’t have occurred on a better season for the team.
19) Jerry Koosman, 1968
Jerry Koosman did something amazing. By many measurements, his best year was his first. Koosman had a small sampling in the majors during the 1967 season. The following year qualified as his rookie campaign. Koosman went 19-12 with a 2.08 ERA. He’d end up 13th in the Cy Young race and the runner-up for the Rookie of the Year, just barely, when Johnny Bench beat him for the honor. A coin toss might have been the decider for some voters as both NL rookies had a case. Koosman was later the Cy Young runner-up in 1976. Compared to 1968, his freshman year was the better of the two.
18) David Cone, 1988
Who says wins don’t matter? In 1988, David Cone went a remarkable 20-3. He wasn’t vulturing wins thanks to the help of a strong offense. Cone pitched to a 2.22 ERA while finishing third in the Cy Young race and 10th in the MVP vote. A somewhat underrated pitcher whose career spanned the lighter hitting 1980s through the Steroid Era of the 1990s, this first full season in a Mets uniform was a preview of the strikeout machine he’d later become. Fanning 212, he’d later manage to lead the league in 1990 and 1991. The ERA in 1988 was about a full run better making this the more worthy campaign.
17) Pete Alonso, 2019
Pete Alonso posted some of the most unique statistics in Mets history. The power is unmatched in a single season and career. His rookie season in 2019 featuring 53 home runs and 120 RBI also included a 5.4 bWAR and a career-high .941 OPS. The record-setting debut season out of Alonso was more than enough to make a lasting impression on Mets fans who will never stop loving him. Alonso, like some others on this list, gets bonus points for doing it as a rookie. Those 53 home runs will be tough for a veteran, let alone a player with no MLB experience, to ever match. He became the Mets home run king for a reason. His power is unmatched from just the eye test.
16) Juan Soto, 2025
Statistically impressive, the only thing missing from Juan Soto’s first year with the Mets was purpose. The team collapsed late despite Soto putting together yet another one of his token MVP-caliber seasons. Along with hitting 43 home runs and posting a league-high .396 OBP, Soto stole 38 bases. His previous single-season high was 12. Truly a one-of-a-kind type of year, the only reason this isn’t higher is because the defense slowed him down. It was the type of year to build off of while making his record-setting contract worth it to Steve Cohen.
15) Francisco Lindor, 2024
Francisco Lindor’s MVP runner-up season in 2024 needs to be experienced to fully understand. He started off as poorly as the team and managed to quite literally lead the club to the NLCS. His first 30/30 season which includes his time in Cleveland was far more complicated than just looking at the .844 OPS. Lindor was a leader and with another Gold Glove-caliber season at shortstop, managed to put together a 6.8 bWAR season. Nothing about the season was statistically insane yet Lindor seemed to do a little bit of everything well.
14) Darryl Strawberry, 1987
Strangely, the best season of Darryl Strawberry’s career with the Mets took place in a non-playoff campaign. The 1987 Mets were good, but not good enough. Strawberry set new career highs with 39 home runs and 104 RBI. Slashing .284/.398/.583 with 36 stolen bases, it was maybe the most complete year Strawberry had as an offensive player. Although he’d lead the league in multiple offensive categories in 1988, many of his 1987 totals were superior. Crossing 30 home runs and 100 RBI for the first time in his career, it was a bit of a transition from Strawberry being one of the star players to be the signature member of the Mets.
13) Bernard Gilkey, 1996
Mets fans who weren’t familiar with Bernard Gilkey’s work might assume he was always one of the better middle of the order hitters. Arriving via trade with the St. Louis Cardinals prior to the 1996 season, Gilkey cranked it up to a whole new level. It feels appropriate that he’d later make a cameo in Men in Black because Gilkey’s numbers were unworldly. He slashed .317/.393/.562 with 44 doubles, 30 home runs, and 117 RBI. The doubles are still the most of any Mets player in a single-season. The 8.1 bWAR became the best in Mets history by a position player. Created by both his bat and glove, Gilkey led the league with 18 assists, 4 double plays, 309 putouts, and ranked as the best at his position in range factor.
12) Tom Seaver, 1975
You knew Tom Seaver was coming eventually. His 1975 season earned him his third and final Cy Young Award. He probably could have had more. This season was a 7.8 bWAR campaign that had him going 22-9 with a 2.38 ERA and a league-leading 243 strikeouts. Compared to most players, it’s incredible. On the list of Seaver performances, this one is easy to overlook because even one of his non-Cy Young winning years was better. Don’t worry. Tom Terrific is all over this list with several seasons that were even better.
11) Tom Seaver, 1969
When it comes to Mets greatness, Tom Seaver is the “you haven’t seen the last of me!” in franchise history. The 1969 season ended with a championship for the Mets. In the regular season, Seaver won a franchise-record 25 games while on his way to his first Cy Young and an MVP runner-up. Neither the 2.21 ERA nor 208 strikeouts would set personal bests. This might have been the most rewarding individual season of Seaver’s career yet it falls short of his best by quite a couple. At least he got winning the big one out of the way relatively early.
10) Jacob deGrom, 2019
Speaking of Cy Young Mets seasons, Jacob deGrom got his second in 2019. His 7.2 bWAR led the league as did the 255 strikeouts. By this point, greatness was something Mets fans weren’t demanding from deGrom, it was expected. A good length away from some of those other memorable Mets seasons by pitchers like Tom Seaver, his 2.43 ERA doesn’t even do him justice for how dominant he was for his second straight season as the best pitcher in the sport. Sadly, this would end up as his final full season in a Mets uniform due to a pandemic as well as injuries in 2021 and 2022.
9) Mike Piazza, 2000
Mike Piazza had big years, moments, and numbers with the Mets. Because his defense behind the plate was never good, stats like WAR don’t rank quite as high as some others. The 2000 season was big regardless as Piazza hit .324/.398/.614 with a 1.012 OPS. The OPS was the largest in any full season for a Mets player. The year included 38 home runs and 113 RBI with the real kicker being that he had only 482 at-bats. One of those more underrated qualities about his offensive abilities, he walked 58 times while only going down on strikes 69 times.
8) Howard Johnson, 1989
Howard Johnson led the league in home runs and RBI in 1991, but it was his 1989 season which deserves a spot on this list. Armed with 36 home runs and 101 RBI, Johnson’s speed went on display with 41 stolen bases. It was his second 30/30 season with the Mets. He hit .287 as well, atypical for the .251 he hit while in orange and blue. Never the biggest star on the Mets roster during his best years in the late 1980s and early 1990s, Johnson’s powerful and speedy 1989 campaign was a special one and the best representation of what he had to offer the ball club during his peak seasons.
7) John Olerud, 1998
Each of the three seasons John Olerud spent with the Mets was special in its own way. A franchise-leading .354 batting average helps break the tie. That’s what he hit in 1998, his middle season with the club. Posting a 7.6 bWAR as well, Olerud was the 12th place finisher in the MVP race during a season where you didn’t get much attention if you weren’t hitting home runs. He had 22 with 93 RBI. More like Keith Hernandez leveled up on offense, newer statistics that emphasis on base have helped this season age better. Olerud was never the best first baseman in the league. In Mets history, he’s right there as one of the stronger overall performers.
6) Carlos Beltran, 2006
Carlos Beltran overcame a rough first year with the Mets in 2005 to put together one of the all-time great ones in 2006. The 41 home runs hit by Todd Hundley in 1996 were matched by Beltran. Posting an 8.2 bWAR, he set a new single-season high in franchise history that would only get to enjoy one season at the top. Beltran slashed .275/.388/.594. He had 95 walks and only 99 strikeouts to practically cancel each other out. The only negative about his season was how it ended. The visual of striking out looking to end Game 7 of the NLCS remains one of the first fans often think about when his name or heartbreaking Mets moments are mentioned.
5) David Wright, 2007
No Mets player has ever matched the popularity of David Wright. His 2007 season, an 8.3 bWAR campaign, set a new mark of excellence. This was Captain America at his absolute best. He hit 30 home runs, stole 34 bases, and cruised past 100 runs scored and RBI. He even hit .325 with a .416 OBP. To make sure no check boxes were left unfilled, he won a Silver Slugger and Gold Glove. The team’s collapse in 2007 likely had to do a lot with why he only finished fourth in the MVP.
4) Jacob deGrom, 2018
As much as Jacob deGrom’s ridiculously good 15-start season in 2021 was historic, it wasn’t a complete year. The 2018 season, on the other hand, included 32 starts and a magnificent 1.70 ERA. This was deGrom’s true coming out party. The debate all year was whether or not a pitcher with a losing record could win the Cy Young. He finished at 10-9 to void the conversation and was one vote shy of a unanimous decision for his first time winning the award. The season included multiple highs for deGrom including 269 strikeouts. It was the ultimate one-man army type of season in Mets history where the team was, oftentimes, only worth watching every fifth day.
3) Tom Seaver, 1971
Here’s the most ridiculous detail about the 1971 season for Tom Seaver: he didn’t win the Cy Young. A league-leading 10.2 bWAR wouldn’t have been known at the time, but a 20-10 record and league-best 1.76 ERA as well as 289 strikeouts to overtake every other pitcher in the National League should have been enough. Seaver settled as the runner-up to Ferguson Jenkins who had a 2.77 ERA and a 24-13 record. The race wasn’t even all that close with Jenkins getting 17 first-place votes and Seaver receiving 6. Both the Mets and Chicago Cubs won 83 games so it’s not as if team record mattered at all. In practically any other year, Seaver would have added more hardware to his collection.
2) Tom Seaver, 1973
If you crave Tom Seaver content, you’re in the right place. His 1973 season earned him his second Cy Young. He had a career-best 10.6 bWAR featuring a league-high 2.08 ERA, 18 complete games, and 251 strikeouts. The Mets would sneak into the postseason and then overtake the Big Red Machine Cincinnati Reds on their way to the World Series. The Mets fell short, of course, but the regular season showing by Seaver was valuable at cementing his Hall of Fame legacy. We can even include the playoffs if there was any doubt. Although he was 1-2 overall, he pitched to a 1.62 ERA in the NLCS and had a 2.40 ERA in the World Series. All the Mets were missing was league-average offense to win another championship.
1) Dwight Gooden, 1985
There shouldn’t have been any question as to what the best season by a Mets player was going to be because what Dwight Gooden did in 1985 was one of the greatest in MLB history. The 12.2 bWAR ranks as the 26th best in MLB history. It’s the best after 1913. Gooden went 24-4 with a 1.53 ERA. He led the league in complete games, innings, and struck out 268 batters. Those numbers matter a lot, as does one other one. Gooden was only 20-years-old for the entire season. This is the kind of year that’ll go unmatched by a Mets player until some sort of cosmic shift in the way the game is played or with the rule book. You can safely etch this into stone as the best.
Hall of Famers, players with retired numbers, some completely random yet memorable performances, and even a few active members cracked the list of the best individual Mets player seasons. Records were broken. Memories were made. In a couple of cases, championships were won.

No baseball team has ever made the playoffs with a .500 or worse record in a full season.

ARLINGTON, Texas (AP) — Marcus Semien hit a tiebreaking homer in the eighth inning against his former team and Brett Baty added a pinch-hit grand slam in the ninth as the New York Mets beat the Texas Rangers 7-2 on Wednesday night.



























Rookie right-hander Nolan McLean (12-10) allowed two runs and three hits over seven innings for the last-place Mets (73-85), who have won both games in Texas since ex-interim manager Andy Green was given the full-time position Tuesday.









































The Rangers (78-80) have lost three consecutive games and trail first-place Houston by a half-game in the AL West, with the Astros playing later in Seattle. They own the head-to-head tiebreaker over Texas if the teams finish with the same record.



























Semien, traded by the Rangers to the Mets last November for Brandon Nimmo, launched his 15th homer this season off All-Star closer Jacob Latz (3-4) to give New York a 3-2 lead. Semien’s first homer since Aug. 7 snapped an 0-for-13 slump.



























Latz entered with two on and one out in the seventh, the first time he’s appeared before the eighth inning since April 12.












The Mets took a 2-0 lead in the third when Juan Soto followed Francisco Lindor’s two-out single with his 27th home run off starter Cody Bradford. It was Soto’s sixth homer this year against left-handed pitching.



























After that, Soto was intentionally walked three times — twice with runners on first and second and a left-hander on the mound.












Texas tied the score at 2 in the fifth after McLean retired the Rangers’ first 12 batters. Nimmo, who spent 10 seasons with the Mets, led off with a sharp single to right field. He advanced to second on Ezequiel Duran’s groundout and scored on Jake Burger’s single. Evan Carter drove in the tying run when he beat out a potential double-play grounder.



























New York left the bases loaded in the fifth and seventh after Soto was intentionally walked. He was given another free pass with first base open and two outs in the ninth, but Bo Bichette then walked against Trevor Williams to load the bases before Baty went deep.



























Rookie LHP Zac Thornton (5-5, 3.40 ERA) starts the series finale Thursday afternoon as the Mets look for a three-game sweep. Texas hadn't announced a scheduled starter.

KANSAS CITY, Mo. (AP) — Maikel Garcia had three hits and three RBIs, including a tiebreaking, run-scoring double in the seventh inning, as the Kansas City Royals beat the White Sox 5-4 Wednesday night and delayed Chicago's bid for a postseason berth.












Chicago could have secured its first playoff berth since 2021 with a win over the Royals and a Texas loss to the New York Mets.

Connor Thomas (2-1) struck out one and allowed one hit in two scoreless innings for the win. Steven Cruz struck out two in the ninth and earned his eighth save.

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has four games left before he can put his 2026 Toronto Blue Jays season behind him.
Guerrero, the six-time All-Star who signed the third highest-paid extension in MLB history in April 2025 at $500 million, has hit just nine home runs and slugged .359 to date for a career-low .695 OPS to date.
The Blue Jays, winners of the American League pennant this past season, where Guerrero was a major factor in reaching the World Series, were mathematically eliminated from this year’s postseason race as they hold a 77-81 record entering Wednesday.
